## Overview

When a parasitoid or predator is released against a crop pest, where will it
be in a year? iPyDisp [@Agboka2024] is a desktop tool that answers with a
cellular automaton on a map:

- the region is cut into a grid of cells about a kilometre or more across;
- a released agent reaches every cell within its travel distance in one time
  step;
- a cell it reaches is colonised if its environment suits the agent (each
  layer, such as temperature or rainfall, lies within bounds), and only
  exposed if not;
- exposed cells pass the agent on as well.

This implementation is a **reproduction** of the tool's released code. The
model is deterministic, and on the same grid, constraints and release sites
every cell's state at every step equals that of the tool's own functions.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
```

## The grid and the neighbourhood

iPyDisp lays a grid of square cells, `cellsize × 0.00833` degrees across
(about `cellsize` km at the equator), over the region's bounding box, keeps
the cells inside the region, and joins two cells when their centroids are
closer than the travel distance on a sphere of radius 6371 km. With cells of
about 9.3 km and a travel distance of 15 km, each cell's neighbours are its
eight surrounding cells; with 20 km, cells two away in a straight line join
too.

```{julia}
ex = ipydisp_example()
g = ex.grid
[(travel=d, most_neighbours=maximum(length, ipydisp_neighbours(g.lat, g.lon, d)))
 for d in (10, 15, 20, 30)]
```

The example region is an ellipse in central Kenya with one synthetic
environmental layer: cells are suitable when it exceeds 0.3.

```{julia}
suitable = ipydisp_suitable(ex.constraints, length(g.lat))
scatter(g.lon, g.lat; zcolor=ex.constraints[1][1], markershape=:square, markersize=3.2,
        markerstrokewidth=0, c=:viridis, aspect_ratio=1, label=false,
        xlabel="longitude", ylabel="latitude", title="environmental layer",
        colorbar_title="value", size=(560, 480))
```

## A release

One release at the centre, followed for 30 steps (months, say).

```{julia}
prob = problem(:ipydisp_dispersal; steps=30)
sol = solve(prob; saveat=1)
counts = ipydisp_counts.(sol.u)
plot(0:30, [getfield.(counts, :colonised) getfield.(counts, :exposed)];
     label=["colonised" "exposed"], lw=2, xlabel="step", ylabel="cells", size=(620, 340))
```

```{julia}
colours = [:lightgray, :gold, :purple]
plot([scatter(g.lon, g.lat; color=colours[sol.u[t + 1].status .+ 1], markershape=:square,
              markersize=2.4, markerstrokewidth=0, aspect_ratio=1, label=false,
              title="step $t", titlefontsize=10, ticks=false)
      for t in (0, 5, 10, 20)]...; layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 260))
```

Colonised cells are purple, exposed ones yellow. The front advances one cell
a step in every direction, through unsuitable cells as well as suitable ones,
since exposed cells pass the agent on. So unsuitable patches do not slow the
spread; they only stay uncolonised.

## How fast it arrives

iPyDisp's validation compares the step at which a known site is first
reached with the time the agent was found there. Without constraints, with
cells joined to their eight neighbours, the step at which a cell is reached
is its Chebyshev distance in cells from the release.

```{julia}
plain = problem(:ipydisp_dispersal; constraints=[], steps=40)
reached = fill(-1, length(g.lat))
let integ = init(plain)
    reached[integ.u.status .== 2] .= 0
    for t in 1:40
        step!(integ)
        reached[(reached .< 0) .& (integ.u.status .== 2)] .= t
    end
end
s = findfirst(==(0), reached)
cheb = [max(abs(g.row[k] - g.row[s]), abs(g.col[k] - g.col[s])) for k in eachindex(reached)]
(all_reached=all(>=(0), reached), equals_chebyshev_distance=reached == cheb)
```

With a longer travel distance the front moves faster. With 20 km, cells two
away in a straight line join, but cells two away on a diagonal do not, so
the front covers the region in fewer steps.

```{julia}
fast = problem(:ipydisp_dispersal; grid=g, neighbours=ipydisp_neighbours(g.lat, g.lon, 20),
               constraints=[], steps=40)
function steps_to_all(prob)
    integ = init(prob)
    t = 0
    while any(==(0), integ.u.status)
        step!(integ)
        t += 1
    end
    return t
end
(travel_15km=steps_to_all(plain), travel_20km=steps_to_all(fast))
```

## Matching the released code

The tool is a desktop application, but its model is three functions and two
loops: the distance, the neighbourhood of the exposed and colonised cells,
the constraint test, the building of the neighbourhood and the update. Run
headless in Python on the same grids, with travel distances of 7.5, 12 and
15 km, two constraint layers and several release sites, they give exactly
the neighbourhoods and the states of every cell at every step that this
model gives, for 25 to 40 steps. The grid built from a bounding box is the
same as well. One difference remains. The tool clips cells at the edge of the
region's polygon and places them at the centroid of their part inside. Here a
cell is kept or dropped whole.

## Deviations from the source

```{julia}
foreach(d -> println("- ", d), model_info(:ipydisp_dispersal).deviations)
```
